svg.title: Who can reach and change what in AWS
svg.desc: Who can reach and change what in AWS. Everything shown is built. Top left, the administrator, by hand: the IAM user branchbook-admin signs in with aws login. Step A: the administrator runs the CDK app with BRANCHBOOK_ALERT_EMAIL or BRANCHBOOK_GUARDRAILS=true set, so the app includes the administrator's stacks; that switch is enforced by code and workflow. cdk deploy then updates the administrator's stacks: BranchbookAccount in us-east-1, which holds the GitHub OIDC provider, a deploy role per environment and the cost budget, and BranchbookGuardrails in af-south-1, which holds CloudTrail, GuardDuty, AWS Config, Security Hub, IAM Access Analyzer, each environment's CloudFormation execution policy and the permissions boundary. Top right, the pipeline, on a push to main, in two lanes, staging on the left and production on the right; the production lane is the main path. Step 1: the delivery jobs of ci.yml never set BRANCHBOOK_ALERT_EMAIL or BRANCHBOOK_GUARDRAILS, so their CDK app never holds the administrator's stacks; enforced by code and workflow. aws-connection-check.yml, run by hand, also declares either environment. Step 2, the GitHub environments: staging admits main only and needs no approval; production admits main only and needs an approval, which administrators cannot bypass; enforced by GitHub settings. Step 3, each environment's deploy role, branchbook-github-deploy-staging or branchbook-github-deploy-production: its trust policy is an exact match (StringEquals), aud sts.amazonaws.com and sub naming this repository by ID and that environment alone; its sessions are short; it may assume only its own CDK bootstrap's roles, cdk-bbstg-* for staging and cdk-hnb659fds-* for production, and otherwise only read its own release records, push to and pull from the image repository and, on staging, read the synthetic-traffic token; enforced by IAM. Step 4, each environment's CDK bootstrap, qualifier bbstg for staging and hnb659fds for production: its deploy role carries the deploy scope branchbook-cdk-deploy-scope-staging or -production, which denies CloudFormation on the other environment's stacks and on the administrator's; its execution role carries branchbook-cdk-cfn-exec-staging or -production instead of AdministratorAccess, which allows IAM only on that environment's own stacks' roles, and creates a role only with the permissions boundary; enforced by IAM. A red arrow with a cross runs from the staging bootstrap to the administrator's stacks: not allowed, guards 1, 3 and 4 keep the pipeline off these stacks. Gap, not prevented by IAM: both environments share one account, so a stack could reach the other's resources through services the execution policies allow, such as the shared hosted zone; and a merge to main needs no second person's approval. At run time, in each environment, left to right: a browser reaches step 5, AWS WAF, which asks for a CAPTCHA on bookings and cancellations, applies per-address limits and blocks /actuator; then step 6, the load balancer, over HTTPS, whose one target is port 8080, while port 8081, the actuator, is in no target group; both enforced by the network. The Fargate task runs in a private subnet with no public IP and admits port 8080 from the load balancer only; a refused box beside it reads: not allowed, port 8081, the actuator. Below, step 7: the permissions boundary branchbook-permissions-boundary, on every role the app stacks create, denies IAM users and keys, shedding the boundary, assuming other roles, account changes, and tampering with CloudTrail, GuardDuty, AWS Config and Security Hub; enforced by IAM. Step 8: the task signs in to the database as branchbook_app with an IAM token and no password; that role has row privileges only, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, no DDL and no access to Flyway's history, and the master secret goes to the migration task alone; enforced by IAM and PostgreSQL. Legend: built, main path, refused or not allowed, gap or caveat; the pill on each guard names what enforces it: IAM, the network, PostgreSQL, a GitHub setting, or code and workflow.
